claim: Fifteen participants (median age 29 years, range [18–56], 7 male) performed a modified Sternberg working memory task.
source: Fifteen participants (median age 29 years, range [18–56], 7 male, Table 1) performed a modified Sternberg WM task (71 sessions in total, 50 trials each).
evidence: Reported demographic data from the study participants

claim: The task involved 71 sessions in total with 50 trials each.
source: Fifteen participants (median age 29 years, range [18–56], 7 male, Table 1) performed a modified Sternberg WM task (71 sessions in total, 50 trials each).
evidence: Reported experimental design parameters

claim: In the task, items were presented all at once rather than sequentially, thus separating the encoding period from the maintenance period.
source: In the task, items were presented all at once rather than sequentially, thus separating the encoding period from the maintenance period.
evidence: Description of the experimental task design

claim: Participants were instructed to memorize sets of 4, 6, or 8 letters presented for 2 seconds during encoding.
source: In each trial, the participant was instructed to memorize a set of 4, 6, or 8 letters presented for 2 s (encoding).
evidence: Description of experimental task parameters

claim: The number of letters was specific for the memory workload.
source: The number of letters was thus specific for the memory workload.
evidence: Explanation of experimental design rationale

claim: Participants read the letters themselves and heard them spoken at the same time.
source: The participants read the letters themselves and heard them spoken at the same time.
evidence: Description of stimulus presentation method

claim: Participants had difficulties reading eight letters within the 2 s encoding period.
source: Since participants had difficulties reading eight letters within the 2 s encoding period, also hearing the letters assured their good performance.
evidence: Observation of participant behavior during task

claim: Hearing the letters assured participants' good performance.
source: Since participants had difficulties reading eight letters within the 2 s encoding period, also hearing the letters assured their good performance.
evidence: Inference about the effect of auditory presentation on performance

claim: After a delay (maintenance) period of 3 s, a probe letter prompted the participant to retrieve their memory.
source: After a delay (maintenance) period of 3 s, a probe letter prompted the participant to retrieve their memory (retrieval) and to indicate by button press ('IN' or 'OUT') whether or not the probe letter was a member of the letter set held in memory (Figure 1a).
evidence: Description of experimental task design

claim: Participants indicated by button press whether the probe letter was a member of the letter set held in memory.
source: After a delay (maintenance) period of 3 s, a probe letter prompted the participant to retrieve their memory (retrieval) and to indicate by button press ('IN' or 'OUT') whether or not the probe letter was a member of the letter set held in memory (Figure 1a).
evidence: Description of response method in the task

claim: During the maintenance period, participants rehearsed the verbal representation of the letter strings subvocally.
source: During the maintenance period, participants rehearsed the verbal representation of the letter strings subvocally, i.e., mentally replayed the memory items.
evidence: Description of participant strategy during task

claim: Participants had been instructed to employ the subvocal rehearsal strategy.
source: Participants had been instructed to employ this strategy, and they confirmed after the sessions that they had indeed employed this strategy.
evidence: Description of experimental instructions and participant confirmation

claim: Participants confirmed after the sessions that they had employed the subvocal rehearsal strategy.
source: Participants had been instructed to employ this strategy, and they confirmed after the sessions that they had indeed employed this strategy.
evidence: Self-report data from participants

claim: Activation of the phonological loop is a component of verbal working memory as it serves to produce an appropriate behavioral response.
source: This activation of the phonological loop (Baddeley, 2003) is a component of verbal WM as it serves to produce an appropriate behavioral response (Christophel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established working memory models

claim: The mean correct response rate was 91% for both IN and OUT trials.
source: The mean correct response rate was 91% (both for IN and OUT trials).
evidence: Behavioral performance data from the experiment

claim: The rate of correct responses decreased with set size from 97% for set size 4 to 89% for set size 6 and 83% for set size 8.
source: The rate of correct responses decreased with set size from a set size of 4 (97% correct responses) to set sizes of 6 (89%) and 8 (83%) (Figure 1b).
evidence: Behavioral performance data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Across the participants, the memory capacity averaged 6.1 (Cowan's K).
source: Across the participants, the memory capacity averaged 6.1 (Cowan's K, [correct IN rate +correct OUT rate –1]×set size), which indicates that the participants were able to maintain at least six letters in memory.
evidence: Calculated memory capacity metric from behavioral data

claim: Participants were able to maintain at least six letters in memory.
source: Across the participants, the memory capacity averaged 6.1 (Cowan's K, [correct IN rate +correct OUT rate –1]×set size), which indicates that the participants were able to maintain at least six letters in memory.
evidence: Inference from Cowan's K calculation

claim: The mean response time for correct trials (3045 trials) was 1.1±0.5 s.
source: The mean response time (RT) for correct trials (3045 trials) was 1.1±0.5 s and increased with workload from set size 4 (1.1±0.5 s) to 6 (1.2±0.5 s) and 8 (1.3±0.6 s), 53 ms/item (Figure 1c).
evidence: Behavioral timing data from the experiment

claim: Response time increased with workload at a rate of 53 ms per item.
source: The mean response time (RT) for correct trials (3045 trials) was 1.1±0.5 s and increased with workload from set size 4 (1.1±0.5 s) to 6 (1.2±0.5 s) and 8 (1.3±0.6 s), 53 ms/item (Figure 1c).
evidence: Calculated rate of response time increase from behavioral data

claim: Correct IN/OUT decisions were made more rapidly than incorrect decisions (1.1±0.5 s vs 1.3±0.6 s).
source: Correct IN/OUT decisions were made more rapidly than incorrect decisions (1.1±0.5 s vs 1.3±0.6 s).
evidence: Comparison of response times between correct and incorrect trials

claim: Participants performed well in the task and the difficulty of the trials increased with the number of letters in the set.
source: These data show that the participants performed well in the task and that the difficulty of the trials increased with the number of letters in the set.
evidence: Summary inference from behavioral performance data

claim: Analysis focused on correct trials with set size 6 and 8 letters to assure hippocampal activation and hippocampo-cortical interaction.
source: In further analysis, we focused on correct trials with set size 6 and 8 letters to assure hippocampal activation and hippocampo-cortical interaction as shown earlier (Boran et al., 2019).
evidence: Methodological decision based on prior findings

claim: Local field potentials were recorded in the hippocampus.
source: To investigate how cortical and hippocampal activity subserves WM processing, we analyzed the LFP recorded in the hippocampus (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1) together with ECoG from cortical strip electrodes (Figure 2a, Figure 3a and f).
evidence: Description of recording methodology

claim: ECoG was recorded from cortical strip electrodes.
source: To investigate how cortical and hippocampal activity subserves WM processing, we analyzed the LFP recorded in the hippocampus (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1) together with ECoG from cortical strip electrodes (Figure 2a, Figure 3a and f).
evidence: Description of recording methodology

claim: In Participant 1, strong gamma activity (>40 Hz) in the relative PSD occurred in an occipital recording while the participant viewed the letters during encoding (increase >100% with respect to fixation).
source: In an occipital recording of Participant 1 (grid contact H3), strong gamma activity (>40 Hz) in the relative PSD occurred while the participant viewed the letters during encoding (increase >100% with respect to fixation, Figure 2b).
evidence: Power spectral density analysis from occipital electrode

claim: Encoding elicited gamma activity in a temporal recording over auditory cortex (increase >100%).
source: Similarly, encoding elicited gamma activity in a temporal recording over auditory cortex (increase >100%, grid contact C2, Figure 2c), similar as in Kumar et al., 2021.
evidence: Power spectral density analysis from temporal electrode, consistent with prior study

claim: Gamma increased significantly only in temporal and occipital-parietal contacts.
source: Gamma increased significantly only in temporal and occipital-parietal contacts (permutation test with z-score >1.96, Figure 2a).
evidence: Statistical test results on spatial distribution of gamma activity

claim: After the letters disappeared from the screen, activity occurred in the [11 14] Hz range toward the end of the maintenance period in temporal and occipital contacts.
source: After the letters disappeared from the screen, activity occurred in the [11 14] Hz range (high alpha/low beta, Figure 2b) toward the end of the maintenance period in temporal and occipital contacts (permutation test p<0.05, Figure 2d).
evidence: Power spectral density analysis with statistical testing

claim: The temporal scalp EEG of Participant 2 showed activity during encoding and maintenance, albeit at lower frequencies.
source: Similarly, the temporal scalp EEG of Participant 2 (black rimmed disk denotes electrode site T3 in Figure 3a) showed activity during encoding and maintenance, albeit at lower frequencies (Figure 3b); this pattern was found only in scalp EEG and not in ECoG, probably because the strip electrode was not located over auditory cortex.
evidence: Comparison of scalp EEG and ECoG recordings with interpretation

claim: The pattern of activity at lower frequencies was found only in scalp EEG and not in ECoG, probably because the strip electrode was not located over auditory cortex.
source: Similarly, the temporal scalp EEG of Participant 2 (black rimmed disk denotes electrode site T3 in Figure 3a) showed activity during encoding and maintenance, albeit at lower frequencies (Figure 3b); this pattern was found only in scalp EEG and not in ECoG, probably because the strip electrode was not located over auditory cortex.
evidence: Interpretation of difference between recording modalities based on electrode location

claim: In Participant 3, a temporo-parietal recording showed gamma activity when letters appeared and alpha activity ([8 11] Hz) during the maintenance period.
source: In Participant 3, a similar pattern occurred in the PSD of a temporo-parietal recording (most posterior strip electrode contact, Figure 3f), where the appearance of the letters prompted gamma activity and the maintenance period showed alpha activity ([8 11] Hz, Figure 3g).
evidence: Power spectral density analysis from temporo-parietal electrode

claim: In Participant 4, electrode contacts on right parietal cortex showed gamma activity during letter stimulus and alpha activity (8–11 Hz) during maintenance.
source: Similarly, in the electrode contacts on right parietal cortex of Participant 4 (Figure 3k), the letter stimulus elicited gamma activity and the maintenance period showed alpha activity (8–11 Hz, Figure 3l).
evidence: Power spectral density analysis from right parietal electrodes

claim: The site of the participants' maintenance activity coincides with the generator of scalp EEG that was found in the parietal cortex for the same task.
source: The site of the participants' maintenance activity coincides with the generator of scalp EEG that was found in the parietal cortex for the same task (Michels et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparison with prior study using the same task

claim: The PSD confirmed the findings of local synchronization of cortical activity during WM maintenance.
source: The PSD thereby confirmed the findings of local synchronization of cortical activity during WM maintenance (Michels et al., 2008; Bidelman et al., 2021; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022).
evidence: Current findings consistent with multiple prior studies

claim: In the hippocampus of all four participants, elevated activity in the beta range ([12 24] Hz) was found toward the end of the maintenance period (increase >100%).
source: In the hippocampus of all four participants, we found elevated activity in the beta range ([12 24] Hz) toward the end of the maintenance period (increase >100%, Figure 2e, Figure 3c, h and m), confirming the hippocampal contribution to processing of this task (Boran et al., 2019).
evidence: Power spectral density analysis from hippocampal recordings, consistent with prior study

claim: The hippocampal beta activity confirms the hippocampal contribution to processing of this task.
source: In the hippocampus of all four participants, we found elevated activity in the beta range ([12 24] Hz) toward the end of the maintenance period (increase >100%, Figure 2e, Figure 3c, h and m), confirming the hippocampal contribution to processing of this task (Boran et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation of hippocampal activity supported by prior study

claim: In Participant 1, high PLV over a broad frequency range was found in contacts over auditory cortex throughout the trial.
source: In Participant 1, we found high PLV over a broad frequency range in contacts over auditory cortex throughout the trial.
evidence: Phase-locking value analysis between hippocampus and auditory cortex

claim: Compared to encoding, maintenance showed enhanced PLV in the theta range between hippocampal LFP and cortical ECoG (PLV=0.4 in contact C3, permutation test p<0.05).
source: Compared to encoding, maintenance showed enhanced PLV in the theta range between hippocampal LFP and cortical ECoG (PLV=0.4 in contact C3, permutation test p<0.05, Figure 2f).
evidence: Statistical comparison of PLV between task periods

claim: PLV in the [4 8] Hz theta range increased significantly with several contacts over auditory cortex.
source: PLV in the [4 8] Hz theta range increased significantly with several contacts over auditory cortex (permutation test p<0.05, Figure 2g).
evidence: Statistical test of PLV spatial distribution

claim: The PLV findings speak for a functional coupling between auditory cortex and hippocampus mediated by synchronized oscillations.
source: This speaks for a functional coupling between auditory cortex and hippocampus mediated by synchronized oscillations (Rezayat et al., 2021).
evidence: Interpretation of PLV results supported by citation

claim: During encoding, the information flow was from auditory cortex to hippocampus with a maximum in the theta frequency range.
source: During encoding, the information flow was from auditory cortex to hippocampus with a maximum in the theta frequency range (dark blue curve in Figure 2h).
evidence: Granger causality analysis results

claim: The net information flow ΔGranger during encoding was significant in the [6 8] Hz range (p<0.05 permutation test against a null distribution).
source: The net information flow ΔGranger (GC hipp→cortex – GC cortex→hipp) during encoding was significant in the [6 8] Hz range (blue bar in Figure 2h, p<0.05 permutation test against a null distribution).
evidence: Statistical test of Granger causality directionality

claim: During maintenance, the information flow in the theta frequency range was reversed from hippocampus to auditory cortex.
source: During maintenance, the information flow in the theta frequency range was reversed (dark red curve), i.e., from hippocampus to auditory cortex (dark red curve in Figure 2h).
evidence: Granger causality analysis results

claim: The net information flow ΔGranger during maintenance was significant in the [5 8] Hz range (p<0.05 permutation test against a null distribution).
source: The net information flow ΔGranger during maintenance was significant in the [5 8] Hz range (red bar in Figure 2h, p<0.05 permutation test against a null distribution).
evidence: Statistical test of Granger causality directionality

claim: The maximal net information flow ΔGranger during encoding occurred from auditory cortex to hippocampus (p<0.05, permutation test).
source: Concerning the spatial spread of the theta GC, the maximal net information flow ΔGranger (GC hipp→cortex – GC cortex→hipp) during encoding occurred from auditory cortex to hippocampus (p<0.05, permutation test, Figure 2i).
evidence: Spatial analysis of Granger causality with statistical testing

claim: During maintenance, the theta ΔGranger was significant from hippocampus to both auditory cortex and occipital cortex (permutation test p<0.05).
source: During maintenance, the theta ΔGranger was significant from hippocampus to both auditory cortex and occipital cortex (permutation test p<0.05, Figure 2j).
evidence: Spatial analysis of Granger causality with statistical testing

claim: In Participant 1, the distribution of high ΔGranger coincides with the distribution of high PLV: both show a spatial maximum to grid contacts over auditory cortex and both appear in the theta frequency range.
source: Interestingly, in Participant 1, the distribution of high ΔGranger coincides with the distribution of high PLV: both show a spatial maximum to grid contacts over auditory cortex and both appear in the theta frequency range.
evidence: Comparison of spatial and frequency patterns between two connectivity measures

claim: The spatial distribution of GC on the grid contacts was tested against a null distribution and found to be statistically significant.
source: We next tested the statistical significance of the spatial spread of contacts with high ΔGranger ([4 8] Hz) during maintenance ([−2 0] s). To provide a sound statistical basis, we tested the spatial distribution of GC on the grid contacts against a null distribution. The activation on grid contacts was reshaped into a grid vector. The spatial collinearity of two grid vectors was captured by their scalar product. We next performed 200 iterations of random trial permutations. For each iteration, we selected two subsets of trials, and we calculated the scalar product between the two vectors corresponding to these subsets. We then tested the statistical significance of the scalar product (Figure 2k). The true distribution (red) is clearly distinct from the null distribution (gray, blue bar marks the 95th percentile).
evidence: Statistical permutation test of spatial distribution

claim: The analogous statistical procedure for PSD, PLV, and GC during encoding gave equally significant results in all cases.
source: The analogous procedure was performed for PSD (Figure 2a and d), PLV (Figure 2g), and GC during encoding (Figure 2i), which gave equally significant results in all cases.
evidence: Statistical testing across multiple measures

claim: In Participant 2, the time course of GC between auditory cortex and hippocampus followed the same pattern as in Participant 1.
source: Similarly in Participant 2, the time course of GC followed the same pattern between auditory cortex (anterior strip electrode contact in Figure 3a) and hippocampus (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: Replication of Granger causality pattern in second participant

claim: Participant 3 had an electrode contact over left visual cortex, indexed by strong gamma activity in the most posterior contact of the strip electrode.
source: Among the participants that had both LFP and temporo-parietal ECoG recordings, Participant 3 had an electrode contact over left visual cortex; the sensory localization was indexed by the strong gamma activity in the most posterior contact of the strip electrode (Figure 3g).
evidence: Electrode localization based on functional response

claim: The time course of information flow between visual cortex and hippocampus in Participant 3 followed the same pattern as described for the auditory cortex.
source: The time course of information flow between visual cortex and hippocampus (Figure 3i and j) followed the same pattern as described for the auditory cortex above.
evidence: Granger causality analysis showing similar pattern in visual cortex

claim: The pattern of information flow appeared with LFP recorded from right hippocampus in Participant 3.
source: Interestingly, the pattern appeared with LFP recorded from right hippocampus in Participant 3 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Observation of pattern in contralateral hippocampus

claim: In Participant 4, recordings from the right cortical hemisphere did not show significant GC between LFP and ECoG during task performance.
source: However, in Participant 4, the recordings from the right cortical hemisphere (Figure 3k) did not show significant GC between LFP and ECoG during task performance (Figure 3n and o).
evidence: Absence of significant Granger causality in right hemisphere

claim: Letters were encoded with information flow from sensory cortex to hippocampus in recordings from the left cortical hemisphere.
source: Thus, we showed in recordings from the left cortical hemisphere that letters were encoded with information flow from sensory cortex to hippocampus; conversely, the information flow from hippocampus to sensory cortex indicated the replay of letters during maintenance.
evidence: Summary of Granger causality findings across participants

claim: The information flow from hippocampus to sensory cortex indicated the replay of letters during maintenance.
source: Thus, we showed in recordings from the left cortical hemisphere that letters were encoded with information flow from sensory cortex to hippocampus; conversely, the information flow from hippocampus to sensory cortex indicated the replay of letters during maintenance.
evidence: Interpretation of Granger causality findings

claim: Beamforming was used to reconstruct the EEG sources during encoding and maintenance for each of the 15 participants.
source: We used beamforming (Oostenveld et al., 2011) to reconstruct the EEG sources during encoding and maintenance for each of the 15 participants (Table 1).
evidence: Description of source reconstruction methodology

claim: In each participant, the proportion of significant sources in the left hemisphere exceeded 80% of all significant sources.
source: In each participant, the proportion of significant sources in the left hemisphere exceeded 80% of all significant sources.
evidence: Statistical analysis of source lateralization

claim: Across all participants, the spatial activity pattern during both encoding and maintenance showed the highest significance in frontal and temporal areas of the left hemisphere.
source: Across all participants, the spatial activity pattern during both encoding and maintenance showed the highest significance in frontal and temporal areas of the left hemisphere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Group-level spatial analysis of EEG sources

claim: The mean GC spectra between hippocampus and EEG beamforming sources in auditory cortex resembled the GC spectrum for ECoG in the theta frequency range ([4 8] Hz).
source: We first calculated the GC between hippocampus and the EEG beamforming sources in the auditory cortex. We found that the mean GC spectra resembled the GC spectrum for ECoG in the theta frequency range ([4 8] Hz, Figure 4a).
evidence: Comparison of Granger causality between EEG sources and ECoG

claim: During encoding, the net information flow was from auditory cortex to hippocampus (p<0.05, group cluster-based permutation test).
source: During encoding, the net information flow was from auditory cortex to hippocampus (light blue curve – dark blue curve, blue bar, p<0.05, group cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: Group-level statistical test of Granger causality directionality

claim: During maintenance, the net information flow was reversed from hippocampus to auditory cortex (p<0.05, group cluster-based permutation test).
source: During maintenance, the net information flow was reversed (dark red curve – light red curve, red bar, p<0.05, group cluster-based permutation test), i.e., from hippocampus to auditory cortex.
evidence: Group-level statistical test of Granger causality directionality

claim: The pattern of bidirectional information flow appeared with LFP recorded from the right hippocampus in several participants.
source: Interestingly, the pattern appeared with LFP recorded from the right hippocampus in several participants (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Observation of pattern in contralateral hippocampus across multiple participants

claim: A similar GC pattern emerged when using the signals from left temporal scalp electrodes but was eliminated when using a Laplacian derivation.
source: A similar GC pattern emerged when using the signals from left temporal scalp electrodes but was eliminated when using a Laplacian derivation.
evidence: Comparison of different EEG referencing methods

claim: Both for ECoG and EEG beamforming sources, GC showed the same bidirectional effect in theta between auditory cortex and hippocampus.
source: Thus, both for ECoG and EEG beamforming sources, GC showed the same bidirectional effect in theta between auditory cortex and hippocampus.
evidence: Summary of consistent findings across recording modalities

claim: During encoding, the mean information flow was strongest from auditory cortex to hippocampus (ΔGranger=−0.049, p=0.0009, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: During encoding, the mean information flow was strongest from auditory cortex to hippocampus (ΔGranger=−0.049, p=0.0009, Kruskal-Wallis test, Figure 4b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of information flow across brain regions

claim: For all other areas during encoding, the mean ΔGranger was also from cortex to hippocampus but the effect was weaker (mean ΔGranger = [–0.03 0]).
source: For all other areas, the mean ΔGranger was also from cortex to hippocampus but the effect was weaker (mean ΔGranger = [–0.03 0], Dunn's test, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical comparison across brain regions

claim: During maintenance, the strongest information flow appeared from hippocampus to auditory cortex (ΔGranger=0.034, p=0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
source: During maintenance (Figure 4c) the information flow was reversed. While all areas had information flow from hippocampus to cortex (ΔGranger = [0.02], Dunn's test, Bonferroni corrected), the strongest flow appeared from hippocampus to auditory cortex (ΔGranger=0.034, p=0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: Statistical comparison of information flow across brain regions

claim: All areas had information flow from hippocampus to cortex during maintenance (ΔGranger = [0.02]).
source: During maintenance (Figure 4c) the information flow was reversed. While all areas had information flow from hippocampus to cortex (ΔGranger = [0.02], Dunn's test, Bonferroni corrected), the strongest flow appeared from hippocampus to auditory cortex (ΔGranger=0.034, p=0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: Post-hoc statistical comparison across brain regions

claim: The reversal of ΔGranger appeared in all 15 participants individually.
source: The reversal of ΔGranger appeared in all 15 participants individually (Figure 4d).
evidence: Individual participant analysis showing consistent pattern

claim: The ΔGranger between hippocampus and auditory cortex was negative during encoding and positive during maintenance in the theta frequency range (p=4.1e-10, paired permutation test).
source: We averaged ΔGranger for each participant in the [4 8] Hz theta frequency range. The ΔGranger between hippocampus and auditory cortex, was negative during encoding and was positive during maintenance in the theta frequency range (p=4.1e-10, paired permutation test).
evidence: Statistical test of directionality reversal across participants

claim: The directionality and its reversal was missing for all other areas, e.g., lateral prefrontal cortex (p=0.16, paired permutation test).
source: The directionality and its reversal was missing for all other areas, e.g., lateral prefrontal cortex (p=0.16, paired permutation test, Figure 4e).
evidence: Statistical test showing specificity of effect to auditory cortex

claim: All analyses up to this point were performed on correct trials only.
source: Of note, all analyses up to here were performed on correct trials only.
evidence: Description of analysis approach

claim: For incorrect trials, the net information flow ΔGranger from auditory cortex to hippocampus did not show the same directionality in all participants and did not reverse in direction (p=0.37, paired permutation test).
source: Finally, we established a link between the participants' performance and ΔGranger. For incorrect trials, the net information flow ΔGranger from auditory cortex to hippocampus did not show the same directionality in all participants and did not reverse in direction (p=0.37, paired permutation test, Figure 4f).
evidence: Statistical comparison between correct and incorrect trials

claim: The effect of directional information flow reversal was equally present for a balanced subset of correct trials (p<0.0005).
source: Since participants performed well (median performance 91%), we balanced the numbers of correct and incorrect trials. We calculated the GC in a subset of correct trials (median of 200 permutations of a number of correct trials that equals the mean percentage of incorrect trials=10%); the effect was equally present for the subset of correct trials (p<0.0005).
evidence: Statistical test with balanced trial numbers

claim: Timely information flow, as indexed by GC, is relevant for producing a correct response.
source: This suggests that timely information flow, as indexed by GC, is relevant for producing a correct response.
evidence: Inference from comparison of correct and incorrect trials

claim: Working memory describes our capacity to represent sensory input for prospective use.
source: Working memory (WM) describes our capacity to represent sensory input for prospective use (Baddeley, 2003; Christophel et al., 2017).
evidence: Definition supported by citations to established literature

claim: Maintaining content in WM requires communication within a widespread network of brain regions.
source: Maintaining content in WM requires communication within a widespread network of brain regions.
evidence: General statement about working memory based on established knowledge

claim: The anatomical basis of WM was shown noninvasively with EEG/MEG.
source: The anatomical basis of WM was shown noninvasively with EEG/MEG (Michels et al., 2008; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Tuladhar et al., 2007; Polanía et al., 2012; Näpflin et al., 2008; Bidelman et al., 2021; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022; Hsieh and Ranganath, 2014) and invasively with intracranial local field potentials (LFP; Cogan et al., 2017; Raghavachari et al., 2001; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Maris et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2010; Leszczyński et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2018a; Johnson et al., 2018b; Boran et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018) and single-unit recordings (Boran et al., 2019; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018; Kamiński et al., 2017; Kornblith et al., 2017; Rutishauser et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by multiple citations

claim: The anatomical basis of WM was shown invasively with intracranial local field potentials.
source: The anatomical basis of WM was shown noninvasively with EEG/MEG (Michels et al., 2008; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Tuladhar et al., 2007; Polanía et al., 2012; Näpflin et al., 2008; Bidelman et al., 2021; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022; Hsieh and Ranganath, 2014) and invasively with intracranial local field potentials (LFP; Cogan et al., 2017; Raghavachari et al., 2001; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Maris et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2010; Leszczyński et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2018a; Johnson et al., 2018b; Boran et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018) and single-unit recordings (Boran et al., 2019; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018; Kamiński et al., 2017; Kornblith et al., 2017; Rutishauser et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by multiple citations

claim: The anatomical basis of WM was shown with single-unit recordings.
source: The anatomical basis of WM was shown noninvasively with EEG/MEG (Michels et al., 2008; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Tuladhar et al., 2007; Polanía et al., 2012; Näpflin et al., 2008; Bidelman et al., 2021; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022; Hsieh and Ranganath, 2014) and invasively with intracranial local field potentials (LFP; Cogan et al., 2017; Raghavachari et al., 2001; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Maris et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2010; Leszczyński et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2018a; Johnson et al., 2018b; Boran et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018) and single-unit recordings (Boran et al., 2019; Schwiedrzik et al., 2018; Kamiński et al., 2017; Kornblith et al., 2017; Rutishauser et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by multiple citations

claim: In cortical brain regions, WM maintenance correlates with sustained neuronal oscillations, most frequently reported in the theta-alpha range ([4 12] Hz).
source: In cortical brain regions, WM maintenance correlates with sustained neuronal oscillations, most frequently reported in the theta-alpha range ([4 12] Hz; Michels et al., 2008; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Tuladhar et al., 2007; Polanía et al., 2012; Näpflin et al., 2008; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022; Hsieh and Ranganath, 2014; Cogan et al., 2017; Raghavachari et al., 2001; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Maris et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2010; Leszczyński et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2018a; Johnson et al., 2018b; Boran et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022) or at even lower frequencies (Kumar et al., 2021; Rezayat et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by multiple citations

claim: WM maintenance has been associated with oscillations at even lower frequencies than theta-alpha.
source: In cortical brain regions, WM maintenance correlates with sustained neuronal oscillations, most frequently reported in the theta-alpha range ([4 12] Hz; Michels et al., 2008; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Tuladhar et al., 2007; Polanía et al., 2012; Näpflin et al., 2008; Pavlov and Kotchoubey, 2022; Hsieh and Ranganath, 2014; Cogan et al., 2017; Raghavachari et al., 2001; Rizzuto et al., 2003; Maris et al., 2011; van Vugt et al., 2010; Leszczyński et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2018a; Johnson et al., 2018b; Boran et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022) or at even lower frequencies (Kumar et al., 2021; Rezayat et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by citations

claim: In the hippocampus, WM maintenance was associated with sustained theta-alpha oscillations.
source: Also in the hippocampus, WM maintenance was associated with sustained theta-alpha oscillations (van Vugt et al., 2010; Boran et al., 2019).
evidence: Summary of prior research supported by citations

claim: Persistent neuronal firing was reported during the absence of sensory input, indicating the involvement of the medial temporal lobe in WM.
